7.160. Panama asserts that its MRL for oxamyl in strawberries was based on the European Union's
MRL, which corresponded to the lower limit of analytical quantification. Panama adds that "neither
the Codex nor the United States considered that the scientific evidence was sufficient to establish
an MRL for oxamyl in strawberries that was safe for human consumption."478
7.161. The record contains information about the imposition or absence of MRLs for oxamyl in
strawberries in the United States, the European Union, and the Codex.479 The Panel notes that, as
Panama indicates, MRLs "are not a substitute for risk" but an "instrument" through which Members
can address a specific risk.480 MRLs represent a reference value for the highest acceptable level of a
pesticide residue in a product from a crop to which that pesticide can be applied, which is why they
are an import requirement for that product. The Panel understands that MRLs result from risk
assessments and that MRLs already established for a pesticide may inform a Member's decision on
what MRL to impose in relation to that pesticide. In particular, the Codex MRLs, as international
recommendations, may serve as a guide.481
7.162. In this regard, information on the existence or values of MRLs for oxamyl in strawberries
from the relevant international organizations or other Members could be relevant to the risk
management phase, in particular, to the adoption of an MRL for this pesticide. The Panel does not
rule out that an MRL value and the considerations that led to its establishment may be relevant to
a risk assessment, especially when such considerations are reflected in a risk assessment. However,
the record contains no information on why there is no MRL for oxamyl in the United States or the
Codex.482 It also contains no explanation of the MRL for oxamyl in strawberries in the
European Union, although it is understood that 0.01 mg/kg corresponds to the lower limit of
analytical quantification achieved with the detection techniques available at that time.483 Thus, in
this case, the Panel does not consider that the existence of an MRL for oxamyl in strawberries in the
European Union and the absence of such an MRL in the United States and the Codex is, in itself,
proof of a situation of insufficient relevant scientific evidence for the assessment of the risk in
question.

7.163. With respect to the sufficiency of the scientific evidence, the main point of contention

7.164. Panama asserts that its MRL operated in conjunction with the fact that oxamyl is not

7.165. Costa Rica considers that, when establishing an MRL, the importing country has no reason
to consider the legislation of exporting countries on the use of the pesticide. Costa Rica adds that,

that the detected instances of non-compliance at issue have called this scientific evidence "into

7.166. As mentioned in paragraph 7.153 above, in the Panel's view, the product processing
regulations and relevant controls in the country of origin are elements relevant to a food safety risk
assessment. The Panel bases this understanding on, inter alia, the appendix to Guidelines
CAC/GL 47-2003 on the relevant information for assessing the level of risk associated with an
imported food. These Guidelines state that the adequacy of processing controls in place in the
exporting country is determined on the "evidence[] [of] its laws, regulations and other policies"; and
that the ability to effectively enforce food safety requirements is established according to what "may
be verified by audits and on-site visits by the competent authority of the importing country".486 The
Panel therefore understands that the relevant risk assessment would take into account (a) the laws,
regulations and other policies of the exporting Member; and (b) the verification at origin carried out
by the authorities of the importing Member.

7.185. The Panel observes that, although Panama asserts that the detections called into question
its conclusions on the risk, its arguments confirm that the detection details constitute relevant
information for the assessment of the risk. The Panel refers to Panama's arguments that cases of
non-compliance with MRLs "constitute, by definition, evidence of a risk that is higher than a
Member's ALOP", and that the levels detected, together with other pieces of information, point to a
higher risk of exposure and ingestion for Panamanian consumers.525
7.186. The Panel recalls that Article 5.7 of the SPS Agreement covers situations where the importing
Member could not arrive at a sufficiently objective conclusion in relation to risk.526 Such situations
are different from those where, due to changes in circumstances, the Member needs to revise its
risk assessment. In the latter case, the Member could reach objective conclusions about the risk,
even though these conclusions differ from those arrived at previously. In the Panel's view, in this
case, the detected level does not affect Panama's ability to perform a risk assessment on the basis
of the available pertinent information, which includes the information on oxamyl and its effects on
human health, the information on Costa Rica's controls, and the details of the detection in question.
7.187. Given that the MRL is defined as the highest level of a pesticide residue that is legally
tolerated in food when pesticides are applied correctly in accordance with GAP527, the Panel
understands that non-compliance with an MRL may indicate that GAP have not been followed in the

7.224. In previous disputes, it has been considered that Article 5 and Annex A of the SPS Agreement

7.225. In the light of the foregoing, the Panel considers that "pertinent information" within the
meaning of Article 5.7 does not refer exclusively to information that addresses the particular risk in
question, but may also refer to information relating to the management of that risk. Thus, in the
Panel's view, Article 5.7 would not exclude international standards of a general nature that address
the management of a particular situation, such as the adoption of measures in situations of non-
conformity, although such standards do not specifically refer to the product or risk (pest or
contaminant) in question that the Member seeks to mitigate.

7.246. Guidelines CAC/GL 26-1997 indicate that, in the event of non-conformity with food safety
requirements, the measures implemented by the importing country should be proportionate to the
degree of risk and cumulative, if necessary.652 This means that the Guidelines recommend first
implementing a measure and then, if justified, imposing additional measures to increase the degree
of trade restrictiveness.
7.247. Moreover, the fact that Guidelines CAC/GL 47-2003 refer, first, to enhanced controls of the
establishment involved, beside other actions; second, to controls of other establishments where
there is evidence of a "systemic problem"653; and, third and lastly, to the suspension of the
importation of the food from the country, illustrates the order in which, according to the Codex, the
mitigation measures should be applied. It should be stressed that Guidelines CAC/GL 47-2003
indicate that the suspension of imports "should be reserved only" for situations involving a "serious
food safety risk".654 The same Guidelines also state that a "serious … risk" is one that "has not been
managed by other means", since this is the phrase that immediately follows and qualifies "serious
… risk".655 The Panel understands that these considerations also apply when adopting a suspension
in "the most serious or persistent cases" within the meaning of Guidelines CAC/GL 26-1997, given
that the two Guidelines provide supplementary guidance on the same subject and there is nothing
in them that contradicts this understanding.656

and are being implemented effectively".657 The Panel considers that this paragraph supports the
interpretation that the Guidelines indicate the order in which measures should be adopted once an

7.249. In the Panel's view, the context in which the term "grave" ("serious")658 appears in both
Guidelines indicates that a serious case of non-conformity or a "serious food safety risk" would be
an instance where other mitigation measures have not worked. Contrary to what Panama asserts,
the Codex Guidelines note that, for a risk to be qualified as serious and for the importing country to
be able to decide to suspend imports, the country should first attempt to manage the risk through
other measures. In this regard, suspension would be understood as a measure of last resort, as
Costa Rica describes it. The Panel does not consider it necessary to rule on the degree to which the
Guidelines must be followed, based on the use of the terms "may" and "should", in order to
determine whether Measure 1 was adopted on the basis of said Guidelines. While the Guidelines do
provide Panama with flexibility in determining which measure to impose based on its assessment of
the circumstances, in the Panel's view, it is evident from these Guidelines that the suspension of
imports is reserved for "serious" cases or cases involving a "serious risk".659
7.250. In this case, Panama has not responded to the detections of non-conformity by implementing
measures in a incremental and cumulative manner. On the contrary, Panama has resorted to the
most restrictive measure, without first attempting to manage the risk by other means. Panama does
not dispute that Measure 1 was the first and only risk management measure that it adopted when
oxamyl residues were detected at levels higher than its relevant MRL in two shipments of
strawberries from Costa Rica. The Panel considers that the case of non-compliance with the oxamyl
MRL in question does not qualify as "serious" or as involving a "serious risk", within the meaning of
the Guidelines, given that this is the first detection of a non-conformity in two shipments from the
same establishment that was not managed in an incremental manner by, for instance, applying
enhanced controls initially. In this respect, Panama fails to explain how the fact that oxamyl is an
extremely hazardous substance660 could affect the possibility of managing the risk in question by
means other than a suspension of imports. Therefore, the Panel considers that, by adopting a
measure that is tantamount to a suspension of imports of strawberries, Panama failed to follow the
guidance of Guidelines CAC/GL 26-1997 and CAC/GL 47-2003 in relation to the management of non-
compliance cases based on the seriousness of risk.

to a "repeated non-conformity in the same product or in the same category of products" or "history
of non-conformity of those responsible for handling the products". Moreover, the Panel finds it
instructive that Guidelines CAC/GL 47-2003 indicate that, in order to assess the risk associated with

7.268. With respect to the European Union's measure, the Panel refers to Regulation No. 178/2002
of 2002 laying down the general principles and requirements of food law. Both parties invoke
Article 53, entitled "Emergency measures for food and feed of Community origin or imported from a
third country".691 This article establishes that "[w]here it is evident that food or feed ... is likely to
constitute a serious risk to human health, animal health or the environment, and that such risk
cannot be contained satisfactorily by means of measures taken by the Member State(s) concerned",
the European Commission shall immediately adopt one or more of the measures listed therein,
"depending on the gravity of the situation". In the case of food or feed from a third country, these
measures include: (a) suspension of imports of the food or feed in question from all or part of the
third country concerned; (b) laying down special conditions for the food or feed in question from all
or part of the third country concerned; and (c) any other appropriate interim measure.692 Article 54,
entitled "Other emergency measures", provides that Member States may adopt "interim protective
measures" where the Commission has not acted in accordance with Article 53. In another
European Union Regulation, it is explained that Articles 53 and 54 "shall apply where, as a result of
new information or of a reassessment of existing information, pesticide residues or MRLs covered ...
may endanger human or animal health requiring immediate action".693

Relevant legal standard
7.309. Article 5.1 reads as follows:
Members shall ensure that their sanitary or phytosanitary measures are based on an
assessment, as appropriate to the circumstances, of the risks to human, animal or plant
life or health, taking into account risk assessment techniques developed by the relevant
international organizations.
7.310. Pursuant to the text of Article 5.1 of the SPS Agreement, the evaluation of a claim under
this provision has been understood to mean that a panel is required to examine:
a. whether there is a risk assessment762, as appropriate to the circumstances, taking into
account risk assessment techniques developed by the relevant international organizations;
and
b. if there is a risk assessment, whether the SPS measure of the Member concerned is based
on that risk assessment.763
7.311. With regard to the risk assessment, it has been deemed that the review power of a panel is
to determine whether the risk assessment is supported by coherent reasoning and respectable
scientific evidence and is, in this sense, objectively justifiable.764 With regard to the examination of
whether the SPS measure is "based on" the risk assessment, this implies determining whether the
results of that assessment "sufficiently warrant" or "reasonably support" the SPS measure at
issue.765
7.312. Article 5.2, reproduced below, sets forth the elements that must be taken into account when
assessing risks:
In the assessment of risks, Members shall take into account available scientific
evidence; relevant processes and production methods; relevant inspection, sampling
and testing methods; prevalence of specific diseases or pests; existence of pest – or
disease – free areas; relevant ecological and environmental conditions; and quarantine
or other treatment.

7.366. Under the legal standard described above859, the Panel will first identify Panama's ALOP, and
subsequently compare it to the level of protection that would be achieved through the alternative

Panama's ALOP
7.367. The Panel notes that Panama has submitted three different formulations of its ALOP with
respect to Measure 1. In its first written submission, in the context of Article 5.7, Panama expressed
its ALOP with respect to Measure 1 as an "ALOP with the lowest possible risk of adverse effects on
human health".860 After the first substantive meeting, Panama stated that, in the area of plant
health, its ALOP is to "prevent and control, in a comprehensive manner" and, therefore, to totally
avoid "the introduction, establishment, and spread of pests of plants and plant products in the
territory of the Republic of Panama".861 Lastly, following the second substantive meeting, Panama
clarified that its ALOP in the case of Measure 1 is "to minimize the risks of toxic residues in plants
and the environment", as, in its view, is set out in Executive Decree No. 63 of 1997.862
7.368. Costa Rica stated at the outset that Panama's ALOP should address human health and not
plant health863, and subsequently added that, even after Panama's last clarification, Panama's
definition of its ALOP remains ambiguous. Costa Rica emphasizes that, although Panama
acknowledges that Measure 1 refers to sanitary risks, Panama states that its ALOP is "to minimize
the risks of toxic residues in plants and the environment".864
7.369. The Panel notes that the ALOP could be understood as an "objective" that the SPS measure

adverse effects on human health arising from oxamyl in Costa Rican strawberries.868

Measure 1 is inconsistent with Article 2.2 because it is not applied only to the extent necessary to
protect human health.

7.457. In its assessment of this issue, the Panel will examine the evidence in the record, which

7.4.1.2.1.1 Relevant Panamanian regulatory framework
7.458. As provided for in the relevant regulatory framework, two types of cumulative eligibility are
needed to import into Panama products of animal origin that pose both sanitary risks (to human
health) and animal health risks (for example, through the transmission of an animal disease).1022
On the one hand, the party interested in exporting products of animal origin for human and/or animal
consumption to Panama must ascertain whether the product of animal origin it wishes to introduce
into Panama is subject to import requirements issued by AUPSA. If there are import requirements,
the interested party must ascertain whether the sanitary eligibility of countries, regions, zones and
districts and/or the approval of the establishment, production chain and/or processing plant is/are
required.1023 On the other hand, the importer must also obtain an animal health import licence,
which recognizes the animal health eligibility of the country, area or region and the establishment
in question.1024

7.466. Although Costa Rica claims that Panama revoked its sanitary eligibility, there is no evidence

amended expressly to revoke Costa Rica's sanitary eligibility.1051
7.467. The Panel also notes that Panama's regulations provide that AUPSA may only suspend or
revoke a country's sanitary eligibility when: (a) there is evidence of substantial changes in its
sanitary status, in accordance with the notification mechanisms established by international
regulations; or (b) there is scientific or technical evidence conclusively demonstrating
non-compliance with Panama's sanitary regulations.1052
7.468. The Panel finds nothing in the record showing that Panama notified Costa Rica that the cases
provided for in Panama's regulations for the suspension or revocation of sanitary eligibility had
arisen. Neither party states that Costa Rica's sanitary status has changed substantially, or that there
is evidence demonstrating a failure to comply with Panama's sanitary regulations for the dairy and
meat products at issue. In the Panel's view, the foregoing supports the conclusion that Panama has
not revoked Costa Rica's sanitary eligibility.
7.469. In respect of animal health eligibility, the Panel notes that the parties have not presented
such detailed evidence as that concerning sanitary eligibility. Therefore, the record does not indicate
when animal health eligibility was granted to Costa Rica for the products at issue or the Costa Rican
establishments in question. However, it seems clear from the aforementioned regulations that, in
order to import the products at issue into Panama, Costa Rica and its establishments had to have
that eligibility. Therefore, it could be assumed that Panama granted animal health eligibility for these
products at least during the period when these establishments were able to export the products at
issue to Panama. In line with what the Panel has noted so far in respect of sanitary eligibility, there
is nothing in the record to indicate that Panama revoked this animal health eligibility.1053
7.470. In addition to the regulatory framework for sanitary and animal health eligibility, the Panel
also finds elements relevant to its analysis in the regulatory framework for the sanitary approval of
establishments. In particular, the AUPSA Manual for the approval of establishments sets out the
procedure to be followed by establishments, production chains and/or processing plants to obtain
approval to export their products of animal origin for human and/or animal consumption to Panama
and, if applicable, subsequent renewals of sanitary approvals.1054
(2009) (Exhibit PAN-1)). The record does not contain evidence of the granting of sanitary eligibility to
Costa Rica for the following products mentioned by Costa Rica in its first written submission: meat products

7.4.1.2.3 Conclusion regarding the content of Measure 2
7.506. In the light of the foregoing, the Panel finds that Costa Rica has failed to demonstrate that
Panama revoked or ceased to recognize Costa Rica's sanitary/animal health eligibility for the
products in question. Therefore, Costa Rica has failed to discharge its burden of proving that
Measure 2 consists of an import prohibition maintained by virtue of Panama's decision to revoke this
eligibility. In addition, the Panel finds that Costa Rica has demonstrated that Measure 2 consists of
an import prohibition on dairy and meat products from Costa Rica maintained by virtue of the
non-renewal of the sanitary approvals of 16 of the 18 Costa Rican establishments in question.
7.507. Accordingly, the Panel's analysis below is limited to Measure 2, as indicated in the preceding
paragraph.

procedures to check and ensure the fulfilment of SPS measures are "undertaken and completed
without undue delay". The wording of Annex C(1)(a) has been interpreted as a good faith obligation
requiring Members to proceed with their approval procedures as promptly as possible, taking account
of the need to check and ensure the fulfilment of their relevant SPS requirements.1226

7.582. The Panel notes that the phrase "without undue delay" has been interpreted as relating to
both the undertaking and the completion of the procedure and, therefore, if a Member causes undue
delay at any stage in an approval procedure, this would constitute a breach of the first clause of
Annex C(1)(a).1227
7.583. It follows from the text of the provision that the analysis of a claim under the first clause of
Annex C(1)(a) comprises two steps: first, the complainant must establish that there has been a
delay in the undertaking or completion of the procedure; and second, the complainant must establish
that the delay was undue.1228
7.584. The concept of "delay" has been interpreted as "(a period of) time lost by inaction or inability
to proceed".1229 In turn, the concept of "undue" has been interpreted as "going beyond what is
warranted" or "unjustifiable".1230 Thus, it is understood that Annex C(1) requires that approval
procedures be undertaken and completed with no unjustifiable loss of time.1231 In this respect, what
matters is whether there is a legitimate reason, or justification, for a given delay, not the length of
a delay as such.1232
7.585. The determination of whether a procedure has been undertaken or completed "without
undue delay" must be made on a case-by-case basis1233, in light of the nature and complexity of the
procedure to be undertaken and completed.1234 In addition, Members have been deemed not legally
responsible for delays which are not attributable to them. Hence, delays attributable to action, or
inaction, of a complainant must not be held against a Member when a determination is made
regarding whether that Member has undertaken or completed approval procedures "without undue
delay".1235 On the other hand, if the Member did not proceed as expeditiously as could be expected
of it in the specific circumstances of the case, the delay caused in this way would be "undue".1236
7.586. The Panel shares these assessments of the legal standard applicable under Annex C(1)(a)
made in the aforementioned disputes and will proceed with its own assessment on that basis.

7.591. The Panel notes that the parties disagree on whether, as a matter of fact, as at 30 June 2020,
Panama had completed the procedures concerning the sanitary approval renewal requests that
Costa Rica had submitted from 2017 onwards. Contrary to what has been stated by Panama1243,
Costa Rica has not acknowledged that Panama completed the renewal procedures by extending the

period to be examined, as, if Panama completed the renewal procedures on 30 June 2020, the only
period that the Panel should evaluate is that after that date. Otherwise, the Panel should also
examine events prior to 30 June 2020.
7.592. To resolve this issue, the Panel will first examine Panama's regulatory framework to identify
when the renewal procedure is considered to have been completed. In this respect, the relevant
provisions of the AUPSA Manual for the approval of establishments stipulate that, as part of the
approval and renewal procedure, an approval resolution is published and the establishment is added
to the database on the AUPSA web page.1245
7.593. The Panel recalls the stages of the sanitary approval renewal procedure mentioned in
paragraph 7.471 . Pursuant to the Manual, this procedure comprises the following stages: (a) the
request from the interested party; (b) the documentary analysis of the sanitary evaluation; (c) the
audit at origin or on site (where applicable); (d) the evaluation by the Institutional Technical
Commission (CTI); (e) the issuance of a resolution approving or refusing the renewal concerned;
and, once the renewal has been approved, (f) the publication of the approval resolution; and (g) the
inclusion of the establishment on the AUPSA web page.1246 Accordingly, the renewal process begins
with the request from the party interested in exporting, which, in this case, was sent by SENASA to
AUPSA.
7.594. Panama's regulations state that on-site audits may form part of the sanitary approval
renewal procedure. In this respect, the AUPSA Manual for the approval of establishments stipulates
that "AUPSA reserves the right to undertake audits and inspections at origin for the renewal of
establishments, based on its decision in the relevant risk analysis".1247 As mentioned in
paragraph 7.473 above, the Manual also stipulates that AUPSA may request documentary
information from the exporting country on the sanitary conditions of the establishment as part of

7.599. The Panel notes that Article 4 of AUPSA Resolution No. 145-AG-2019, extending the validity
of the sanitary approvals of various Costa Rican establishments, stipulates the need to draw up a
timetable for the on-site audits of the establishments listed therein.1256 Moreover, AUPSA made

7.600. Accordingly, the Panel considers that the following stages must be carried out for the
procedure to renew the sanitary approvals of each of the Costa Rican establishments to be deemed
to have been completed: (a) AUPSA undertakes a documentary analysis of the sanitary evaluation;
(b) AUPSA and other sanitary authorities of Panama undertake on-site audits; (c) the CTI evaluates
and approves the renewal request after checking compliance with the relevant requirements;
(d) AUPSA issues and publishes a resolution renewing the sanitary approval of the establishment
concerned; and (e) AUPSA includes the establishment concerned on its web page.
7.601. With respect to recording the sanitary approval extensions of the establishments awaiting
renewal on the AUPSA web page, Costa Rica considers that publishing this information does not
signify that AUPSA had processed and completed the sanitary approval renewal procedures for the
Costa Rican establishments. Costa Rica adds that, under Panama's regulatory framework,
completing the procedure requires an approval resolution to be issued, which did not happen.1258 In
this respect, Panama considers that the renewal procedure in question was completed each time the
approval of each of the 16 Costa Rican establishments was extended.1259
7.602. The evidence in the record indicates that AUPSA recorded the 2019 and 2020 extensions for
the 16 Costa Rican establishments on its web page.1260 However, the record does not include
documents that confirm that the Panamanian authorities completed the other stages1261 of the
procedure. The Panel does not consider the inclusion of the establishments on the AUPSA web page
to be sufficient to consider the sanitary approval renewal process to have been completed. In
accordance with the Panamanian regulatory framework, the technical evaluation of the substance of
the renewal request is a fundamental component of this procedure. Accordingly, simply recording
the extensions issued on a web page, without providing an examination of the merits of the request,
cannot be considered sufficient to conclude that the procedure in question has been completed. In
the light of the foregoing, the Panel concludes that, as at 30 June 2020, Panama had not completed
the procedure to renew the sanitary approvals of 16 of the 18 Costa Rican establishments in
question.

renew the sanitary approvals of each of the establishments and the establishment of the Panel is
sufficiently long to conclude that Panama failed to proceed in the review of the merits of the sanitary
approval renewal requests or in scheduling or undertaking on-site audits. Accordingly, the Panel
considers that Panama incurred delays within the meaning of Annex C(1)(a) to the SPS Agreement
with respect to the procedures to renew the sanitary approvals of 16 of the 18 Costa Rican
establishments in question.
Whether the delays were "undue"
7.612. The second issue that the Panel will assess in order to determine the consistency of
Measure 2 with Annex C(1)(a) is whether the delays identified in the previous section were undue,
in the sense that there was no justification for them. The Panel recalls that a delay is undue when it
is unjustifiable1292, and that what matters is whether there is a legitimate reason, or justification,
for a given delay, not the length of a delay as such.1293
7.613. Costa Rica identifies three reasons why the delays incurred by Panama are unjustifiable:
(a) the on-site audits were not undertaken for reasons attributable to Panama; (b) the logistical
constraints relating to the COVID-19 pandemic did not prevent Panama from undertaking the on-site
audits before March 2020 or after October 2020; and (c) requiring Costa Rica to complete a new
country sanitary eligibility procedure is not a legitimate justification for the delay.1294

7.4.2.3.2.4 Conclusion on Annex C(1)(a) of the SPS Agreement
7.640. In the light of the foregoing, the Panel concludes that the evidence in the record
demonstrates that Panama incurred delays in the process of renewing the sanitary approvals of the
16 Costa Rican establishments between 2017 and September 2021, when the Panel was established.
7.641. These delays arise from three main aspects: (a) delays in clarifying the information that
Panama required in order to process the renewals, and in conducting the corresponding documentary
review, (b) the failure to conduct on-site audits, which in the case at hand form part of the sanitary
approval renewal procedure, and (c) the failure to issue rulings on the substance of the applications
to renew the sanitary approvals of the 16 Costa Rican establishments.
7.642. With respect to the delays in clarifying the information that Panama required and in
conducting the corresponding documentary review, the Panel considers that these delays were
undue within the meaning of Annex C(1)(a) of the SPS Agreement during the periods
January 2020-March 2020 and June 2020-February 2021, as there is no reason why Panama should
not have informed Costa Rica of the missing information it needed. The Panel further considers that
there are no reasons to justify, during the above periods, the failure to undertake a documentary
review of the information Costa Rica sent to Panama in February 2020.
7.643. With respect to the failure to conduct on-site audits, the Panel considers that these delays
were undue within the meaning of Annex C(1)(a) of the SPS Agreement during the periods
January 2017-March 2020 and October 2020-September 2021, as there is no legitimate justification
for not having carried out the respective audits. The Panel, however, considers that Panama's delays
between March and October 2020 are not undue, as these delays are justified by the measures taken
to address the COVID-19 pandemic.
7.644. With regard to AUPSA's failure to issue rulings, the Panel considers that these delays were
undue within the meaning of Annex C(1)(a) of the SPS Agreement during the periods
January 2017-March 2020 and June 2020-September 2021, taking into account that deadlines in
administrative procedures were partially resumed as of June 2020, following a temporary suspension
between March and June 2020 due to the COVID-19 pandemic.
7.645. In the light of the foregoing, the Panel finds that Measure 2 is inconsistent with Annex
C(1)(a) of the SPS Agreement, because Panama incurred undue delays in the course of the
procedures for renewing the sanitary approvals of 16 Costa Rican establishments.

7.648. The Panel notes that Panama's arguments under Article 23 of the draft articles on

Relevant legal standard
7.658. According to Annex C(1)(c) of the SPS Agreement, Members shall ensure that "information
requirements are limited to what is necessary for appropriate control, inspection and approval
procedures". This obligation, which applies with respect to any procedure to check and ensure the
fulfilment of SPS measures, entails determining the objective of the procedure in question and the
type of information necessary for that procedure.1389 If the evidence in the record demonstrates that
the respondent's requests for information are excessive for the purposes of the procedure in
question, the respondent could be found to have acted inconsistently with Annex C(1)(c).1390
7.659. In the light of the legal standard described above, the Panel will proceed to examine whether
Panama requested more information from Costa Rica than was necessary for the purposes of the
procedure to renew the sanitary approvals of the 16 Costa Rican establishments.

like to continue to introduce into the country.

certification systems of the exporting country and the establishment, production

7.683. The Panel draws two main conclusions from the above comparison. The first is that the model
questionnaires include, in some areas, more detailed questions on topics that are also referred to in
the February 2021 questionnaire. The second is that, in the February 2021 questionnaire, AUPSA
requested information that was much more detailed than the information it usually requests in the
model questionnaires for certain areas, while for others, it requested additional information not
included in the model questionnaires. In the Panel's view, the fact that much of the additional
information requested does not appear in the model questionnaires typically used by Panama,
suggests that this information was not necessary for the purpose of renewing the sanitary approvals.
7.684. The Panel further notes that, in its communications to Costa Rica, AUPSA did not explain
why it needed this information. However, during the current proceedings, Panama stated that the
information requested in February 2021 was necessary owing to the animal health risks posed by
dairy products, such as the transmission of foot and mouth disease. Panama also stated that in 2014
it had requested the Costa Rican authorities responsible for animal health to evaluate these types
of risks, so it should not have come as a surprise to those authorities that animal health information
was requested during a renewal procedure.1516
7.685. The Panel does not consider that Panama's explanations justify the need to request such
detailed information on general aspects of the sanitary system such as those referred to in
paragraph 7.679 above. It is the Panel's understanding that this would be information that was not
clearly related to the animal health concerns raised by Panama in a context where it had a history
of trade with Costa Rica in multiple products and was familiar with the sanitary and veterinary
authorities of its trading partner. Furthermore, as mentioned above, the questionnaire sent on
2 January 2020 contained 51 specific questions on two bovine diseases, and other more general
questions regarding the management of zoonoses and the animal health situation in Costa Rica.
7.686. As explained above1517, the Panel considers that Panamanian law authorizes AUPSA to
request updated information on the sanitary situation of the exporting country, which may include
information about the animal health situation.
7.687. Furthermore, it should be recalled that there is nothing in the record to show that AUPSA
commented on the information that SENASA sent it on 19 February 2020 in response to the
questionnaire of 2 January 2020. If AUPSA believed that the information it requested more than a
year later, in February 2021, was necessary for its evaluation, it could have notified SENASA much
more promptly.1518 AUPSA's lack of action in this respect would tend to confirm that the additional
information requested in February 2021 was not necessary.

7.4.2.3.4.3 Conclusion on Annex C(1)(c) to the SPS Agreement
7.690. In the light of the foregoing, the Panel finds that Measure 2 is inconsistent with Annex C(1)(c)
to the SPS Agreement, because Panama required more information from Costa Rica than was
necessary for the purpose of completing the procedure for renewing the sanitary approvals of the
16 Costa Rican establishments.
7.4.2.3.5 Whether Measure 2 is inconsistent with Article 8 of the SPS Agreement
7.691. Costa Rica requests the Panel to find a violation of Article 8 of the SPS Agreement because
Panama has incurred undue delay and has required more information than is necessary for the
procedures at issue, in breach of Annex C(1)(a) and Annex C(1)(c) to the SPS Agreement.1521
Panama, for its part, contends that Costa Rica has failed to demonstrate that Measure 2 violates
Article 8 of the SPS Agreement.1522
7.692. The Panel notes that Annex C(1) to the SPS Agreement gives meaning and content to
Article 8 of the Agreement.1523 Article 8 establishes the obligation to observe the provisions of
Annex C in the operation of control, inspection and approval procedures. Thus, a failure to observe
the provisions of Annex C implies a breach of Article 8.1524
7.693. The Panel has found that Measure 2 is inconsistent with Annex C(1)(a) to the SPS Agreement
because Panama incurred undue delays in the course of the procedures for renewing the sanitary
approvals of 16 Costa Rican establishments.1525 The Panel has also found that Measure 2 is
inconsistent with Annex C(1)(c) to the SPS Agreement because Panama required more information
from Costa Rica than was necessary for the purpose of completing these procedures.1526
7.694. Consequently, the Panel finds that Measure 2 is inconsistent with Article 8 of the
SPS Agreement, because Panama failed to comply with the provisions of Annex C(1)(a) and

7.4.2.4.1 Order of analysis
7.696. In its panel request, Costa Rica submits a claim that all of the measures at issue are
inconsistent with Article 5.5 of the SPS Agreement, together with a consequential violation of
Article 2.3 of the SPS Agreement.1529 Subsequently, Costa Rica proposes that the Panel first address
its claims under Article 2.3 "because of the broader nature of the non-discrimination obligations"
contained therein, "as opposed to the focus of Article 5.5 on discrimination that may arise in respect
of distinctions in levels of protection".1530 Furthermore, Costa Rica considers that the Panel could
exercise judicial economy with respect to the claims under Article 5.5 if it were to find that
Measures 2 and 3 were inconsistent with Article 2.3.1531 For its part, Panama does not object to

procedures.1532
7.697. The Panel recalls that Article 5 of the SPS Agreement elaborates on the basic obligations
under Article 2 of the Agreement.1533 Previous panels have considered that Article 5.5, which
requires Members to avoid arbitrary or unjustifiable distinctions in the ALOPs they consider to be
appropriate in different situations, when such distinctions result in discrimination or a disguised
restriction on international trade, elaborates on the non-discrimination obligation under
Article 2.3.1534 It follows that in previous disputes where claims were made under both provisions,
panels have sometimes considered Article 5.5 first and concluded that their findings applied to the
claim under Article 2.3.1535 In those disputes where the claim under Article 5.5 was presented as an
alternative claim, or where arguments under Article 2.3 were made first, because of the broader
nature of its obligations, the panels chose to start their assessments with Article 2.3 and exercised
judicial economy with respect to Article 5.5 by finding a violation of Article 2.3.1536
7.698. Given the parties' positions on the order of analysis as stated above1537 and the possibility
of exercising judicial economy, the Panel considers it appropriate to begin its analysis with Costa
Rica's claims under Article 2.3 of the SPS Agreement.

7.4.2.4.2.2 Assessment by the Panel
Relevant legal standard
7.709. Article 2.3 of the SPS Agreement reads as follows:
Members shall ensure that their sanitary and phytosanitary measures do not arbitrarily
or unjustifiably discriminate between Members where identical or similar conditions
prevail, including between their own territory and that of other Members. Sanitary and
phytosanitary measures shall not be applied in a manner which would constitute a
disguised restriction on international trade.
7.710. It is clear from the wording of the provision that Article 2.3 contains two obligations, each
of which corresponds to one of the sentences of Article 2.3:
a. Under the first sentence, Members must ensure that their SPS measures do not arbitrarily
or unjustifiably discriminate between Members where identical or similar conditions
prevail, including between their own territory and that of other Members.
b. Under to the second sentence, Members must ensure that their SPS measures are not
applied in a manner which would constitute a disguised restriction on international
trade.1560
First sentence of Article 2.3 of the SPS Agreement
7.711. In the light of the first sentence of Article 2.3, the complainant is required to demonstrate
three cumulative elements to establish a violation of this obligation:
a. that the SPS measure discriminates between the territories of Members other than the
Member imposing the measure, or between the territory of the Member imposing the
measure and that of another Member;
b. that the discrimination is arbitrary or unjustifiable; and
c. that identical or similar conditions prevail in the territory of the Members compared.1561
7.712. These three elements inform each other. While it has not been deemed that the analysis of
these elements should follow a particular order1562, in previous disputes, panels have begun their
analysis by identifying the relevant conditions, and assessing whether they are identical or similar,
as this is considered to provide a good starting point for an analysis under the first sentence of
Article 2.3.1563
7.713. With respect to the prevalence of identical or similar conditions in the Members compared,
it should be noted that the relevant conditions must be identified, taking into account the specific
nature of the measure at issue and the specific circumstances of the case. This may require
consideration of the SPS measure's stated Annex A(1) "protected interest"1564 or of the specific
SPS risk at issue1565, which relates to an objective pursued under the SPS Agreement. This objective
may inform the "conditions" that must be "identical or similar" under the first sentence of

has been interpreted to exist when different treatment is accorded to Members where identical or
similar conditions prevail.1570 Other provisions that have been referred to when interpreting the term
"discrimination" are Article III:4 of the GATT 1994 and Article 5.5 of the SPS Agreement.1571 Thus,
a measure has been considered to discriminate if it "alters the conditions of competition to the
detriment of products originating in the territories of Members other than the Member imposing the
measure".1572 It has also been held that prohibiting imports of relevant products of one Member,
while permitting imports of relevant products presenting an equivalent level of risk from other
Members, is a "warning signal" of the existence of discrimination, as under Article 5.5 of the
SPS Agreement.1573

also relied on interpretations given to the terms in the context of Article XX of the GATT 1994. As
such, it has been determined that the analysis of this issue "should focus on the cause of the
discrimination, or the rationale put forward to explain its existence".1574 The analysis would therefore
focus on whether the measure at issue bears a "rational connection to" its stated objective.1575

7.782. The Panel recalls that the analysis of whether discrimination is arbitrary or unjustifiable

its existence"1700, taking into account both the provisions relating to the measure's application and
its actual application. The Panel's analysis will therefore focus on whether the discrimination
stemming from Measure 2 bears a "rational connection to" its objective of protecting human or
animal life or health from risks associated with food safety and zoonosis.1701
7.783. The Panel will now proceed to examine whether any of the reasons put forward by Panama
to justify its refusal to extend the sanitary approvals of the Costa Rican establishments on the basis
of an initial documentary assessment, followed by an on-site audit, have a rational connection to
the objective of Measure 2 and the risk addressed by that measure.

with Panamanian sanitary regulations
7.784. The first reason put forward by Panama relates to compliance with its sanitary regulations.
In its communication of 10 July 2020, in which it rejected Costa Rica's request to extend the sanitary
approvals on the basis of a documentary assessment of the 16 Costa Rican establishments, Panama
stated the following: "[a] documentary assessment alone does not satisfy or ensure compliance with
the requirements stipulated in Panama's sanitary legislation to be met by these establishments".1702
However, Panama has not explained why it considers that "a purely documentary review would not
achieve Panama's level of sanitary protection".1703
7.785. In this connection, the Panel notes that Costa Rica did not request a "documentary
assessment alone", as indicated by Panama in its communication to Costa Rica of 10 July 2020.
Costa Rica requested that its establishments be evaluated and approved on a documentary basis,
pending on-site audits at a later date.1704 This same type of evaluation was applied by Panama to
the extensions granted to establishments in Peru and New Zealand.1705

explanation as to why it was possible to accept imports from Peru and New Zealand on the basis of
a documentary assessment and not imports from Costa Rica, taking into account the objective of
Measure 2. In conclusion, the Panel considers that there is no rational connection between the
differential treatment accorded to Costa Rican establishments compared to those in Peru and
New Zealand, on the one hand, and the protection of human or animal life or health from risks
associated with food safety and zoonosis, on the other.

7.793. Lastly, Panama relies on the COVID-19 pandemic to make the completion of approval

7.851. Costa Rica submits that the alternative measure is significantly less restrictive to trade than

7.883. The Panel will now examine whether, in accordance with the legal standard described in
section 7.3.1.1.2.1 above, the SPS Agreement is applicable to Measure 3. In particular, the Panel
will consider whether, as provided for in Articles 1.1 and 1.2 of that Agreement, Measure 3:
(a) constitutes an SPS measure in accordance with the definition given in Annex A to the
SPS Agreement; and (b) may, directly or indirectly, affect international trade.
7.5.1.1.2.2 Whether Measure 3 constitutes an SPS measure within the meaning of
Annex A(1) to the SPS Agreement
7.884. As mentioned in the descriptive part, Measure 3 inactivates the resolution containing
Panama's PIR for Costa Rican pineapple.1836 Taking into account the legal standard described above,
the task of this Panel is to determine whether Measure 3 has been applied to achieve at least one of
the objectives listed in paragraphs (a)-(d) of Annex A(1), which are set out above.1837 In this respect,
the Panel notes that, in Note AUPSA-AG-032-2019, whereby Panama informed Costa Rica of
Measure 3, Panama stated that measure was a "preventive measure".1838 The Note indicates that
the measure would be maintained until Costa Rica provided "further information … on the
phytosanitary status of pineapple production areas, in reference to the pink mealybug pest ... and
other pests indicating their … status" at that time.1839
7.885. Note AUPSA-AG-032-2019 identifies the pest of concern, namely the pink mealybug. It
follows from the Note that Panama associates the risk of this pest with pineapple imports from
Costa Rica, given that Panama inactivated the resolution containing the PIR for pineapple from
Costa Rica after verifying its phytosanitary status in relation to imports of that product.1840 In its
response to this Note, the SFE of Costa Rica confirms that it understands that the measure is the
result of an assessment that determined a risk consisting of the possible presence of pink mealybug
in Costa Rican pineapples.1841 In this regard, the Panel recalls that the pink mealybug is a highly
polyphagous insect that affects a wide variety of plants1842, including pineapple.1843
7.886. In the Panel's view, the notification of Measure 3 to Costa Rica indicates that the measure is
applied because of the risk posed, according to Panama, by Costa Rican pineapples of the
pink mealybug entering Panama.
7.887. Accordingly, the Panel considers that the objective of Measure 3 relates to the objective of
"protect[ing] … plant life or health within the territory of the Member from risks arising from the
entry, establishment or spread of pests", set out in Annex (A)(1)(a) to the SPS Agreement.
7.888. With regard to the type of measure, the Panel considers that Measure 3, which consists of
inactivating the resolution containing the PIR for Costa Rican pineapple, makes it impossible to
import this product. Therefore, in the Panel's view, Measure 3 could qualify as a requirement for the
purposes of Annex A(1).1844 Moreover, as indicated above, even if it is not expressly included in the
list of measures in Annex A(1), a measure may be considered an SPS measure if it is applied to
achieve one of the objectives listed in that provision. Measure 3 meets this requirement and,

7.5.1.1.2.3 Whether Measure 3 may, directly or indirectly, affect international trade
7.889. The Panel considers that, given the nature of the measure, and as explained above in relation

7.5.1.1.3 Conclusion on the applicability of the SPS Agreement to Measure 3
7.890. Having determined that Measure 3 constitutes an SPS measure within the meaning of
Annex A(1)(a) to the SPS Agreement and that it directly affects international trade within the
meaning of Article 1.1 of the Agreement, the Panel finds that the SPS Agreement does apply to this
measure.
7.891. Accordingly, the Panel will examine Costa Rica's claims regarding the scientific basis of the
measure under Articles 5.1, 5.2, 5.3, 2.2, and 5.7 of the SPS Agreement.
7.5.1.2 Claims under Articles 5.1, 5.2, 5.3, 2.2, and 5.7 of the SPS Agreement
7.892. Costa Rica asserts that Measure 3 is inconsistent with Articles 5.1, 5.2, and 5.3 of the
SPS Agreement because it is not based on an assessment, as appropriate to the circumstances, of
the risks to plant life or health. Costa Rica claims that, consequently, Measure 3 is also inconsistent
with Article 2.2 of the SPS Agreement, given that it is not based on scientific principles and is
maintained without sufficient scientific evidence.1846 Moreover, Costa Rica considers that Measure 3
is not covered by the exemption provided for under Article 5.7 of the SPS Agreement because it
does not meet the requirements of this provision.1847 Costa Rica adds that Panama has not rebutted
its prima facie case of the inapplicability of Article 5.7 of the SPS Agreement, nor has it met its
burden of proving that all the requirements of this provision have been met.1848
7.893. Panama, for its part, asserts that Costa Rica has failed to establish a prima facie case that
Panama does not meet the four requirements set out in Article 5.7 of the SPS Agreement.1849
Panama requests the Panel to conclude that Measure 3 is a provisional measure covered by
Article 5.7 and that, consequently, Panama has not acted inconsistently with Articles 2.2, 5.1, 5.2,
and 5.3 of the SPS Agreement.1850
7.894. According to the allocation of the burden of proof under Article 5.7 set forth in
paragraph 7.121 above, the Panel will first examine whether Measure 3 qualifies as a provisional
measure within the meaning of Article 5.7 of the SPS Agreement. Depending on its findings with
respect to that issue, the Panel will decide whether it is necessary to address Costa Rica's claims
under Articles 5.1, 5.2, 5.3, and 2.2 of the SPS Agreement. In this regard, the Panel recalls that
Article 5.7 has been considered a qualified exemption from the obligation under Article 2.2 to not
maintain an SPS measure without sufficient scientific evidence and, by extension, from those under

7.925. In this section, ISPM 11 addresses the following five issues:
a. Identification of pathways for a PRA initiated by a pest
i. ISPM 11 states that "[p]est interception data may provide evidence of the ability of a
pest to be associated with a pathway and to survive in transport or storage".1918 It also
states that entry by natural means should also be assessed.1919
b. Probability of the pest being associated with the pathway at origin
i. The ISPM provides that "[t]he probability of the pest being associated, spatially or
temporally, with the pathway at origin should be estimated" and, to that end, it
includes a non-exhaustive list of factors to consider, namely: (a) prevalence of the
pest in the source area; (b) occurrence of the pest in a life stage that would be
associated with commodities, containers or conveyances; (c) volume and frequency of
movement along the pathway; (d) seasonal timing; and (e) pest management,
cultural and commercial procedures applied at the place of origin (application of plant
protection products, handling, culling, roguing, grading).1920
c. Probability of survival during transport or storage
i. ISPM 11 identifies the following factors to consider: (a) speed and conditions of
transport and duration of the life cycle of the pest in relation to time in transport and
storage; (b) vulnerability of the life stages during transport or storage; (c) prevalence
of pest likely to be associated with a consignment; and (d) commercial procedures
(e.g. refrigeration) applied to consignments in the country of origin, country of
destination, or in transport or storage.1921

management procedures (including phytosanitary procedures)[,] applied to

the pest in question".1922 It also mentions the need to estimate "[t]he probability that
the pest will go undetected during inspection or survive other existing phytosanitary
procedures".1923

7.926. ISPM 11 states that "reliable biological information (life cycle, host range, epidemiology,
survival, etc.) should be obtained from the areas where the pest currently occurs", and that "[c]ase
histories concerning comparable pests can be considered".1926
7.927. Among the examples of the factors to be considered, the ISPM includes the following:
(a) availability, quantity and distribution of hosts in the PRA area; (b) environmental suitability in
the PRA area; (c) potential for adaptation of the pest; (d) reproductive strategy of the pest;
(e) method of pest survival; and (f) cultural practices and control measures.1927
7.928. In the section on probability of establishment, ISPM 11 addresses the following four issues:
a. Availability of suitable hosts, alternate hosts and vectors in the PRA area
i. In this regard, factors to consider according to the ISPM are: (a) whether hosts and
alternate hosts are present and how abundant or widely distributed they may be;
(b) whether hosts and alternate hosts occur within sufficient geographic proximity to
allow the pest to complete its life cycle; (c) whether there are other plant species,
which could prove to be suitable hosts in the absence of the usual host species;
(d) whether a vector, if needed for dispersal of the pest, is already present in the
PRA area or likely to be introduced; and (e) whether another vector species occurs in
the PRA area.1928
b. Suitability of environment
i. ISPM 11 states that factors in the environment (e.g. suitability of climate, soil, pest
and host competition) that are critical to the development of the pest, its host and if
applicable its vector, and to their ability to survive periods of climatic stress and
complete their life cycles, should be identified.1929
c. Cultural practices and control measures
i. According to ISPM 11, where applicable, practices employed during the
cultivation/production of the host crops should be compared to determine if there are
differences in such practices between the PRA area and the origin of the pest that may
influence its ability to establish.1930
ii. Pest control programmes or natural enemies already in the PRA area which reduce the
probability of establishment may also be considered, as may the availability, or lack,
of suitable methods for eradication.1931

7.941. Having examined the 2011 publication, the Panel notes that, of the 30 pages that make up
the publication, only a few lines are devoted to the pink mealybug. These lines report the presence
of the pink mealybug in Fiji for the first time, once on hibiscus and once on pineapple.1950 The rest
of the publication mainly deals with the discovery of new species of mealybug in Fiji. The authors
recall that this polyphagous pest is widespread throughout southern Asia, Australia and Africa, and
that it has spread to many geographic areas in recent years. The authors state that it is a potential
invasive pest of several crops, particularly pineapple.1951 The publication includes a list of mealybug
species recorded in Fiji that indicates that the pink mealybug was found on two of Fiji's islands on
the following host plants: Ficus sp.1952, Hibiscus rosa-sinensis1953 and Ananas comosus
(pineapple).1954
7.942. The authors of this publication do not indicate that their findings question existing scientific
evidence; they merely state that, during their "small survey"1955, they recorded the pink mealybug
pest in Fiji for the first time and that the pest could be potentially very important ecologically and
economically.1956 In the Panel's view, this publication does not question previous scientific evidence
on hosts of the pest, instead it complements existing information on the pest by reporting its
presence on pineapple in Fiji. Given the "highly polyphagous"1957 nature of the pest, detected in
more than 300 plant genera in over 85 families1958, the fact that a scientific publication reports the
detection of the pest on pineapple in Fiji does not appear to call into question the scientific evidence
on the matter, but rather to confirm the pest's polyphagous nature.

in relation to pineapple as a host of the pest stemming from the 2011 publication that Panama claims
to have discovered in 2018.

the pest in Panama through imports of pineapples from Costa Rica. The Panel refers to ISPM 11,
according to which "[p]est interception data may provide evidence of the ability of a pest to be
associated with a pathway and to survive in transport or storage".2024 Accordingly, the Panel sees
no reason to deny the pertinence of the information concerning interceptions of the pest.
7.975. Furthermore, Panama had the information on Costa Rica's phytosanitary status in respect of
the pink mealybug pest at the time Measure 3 was adopted. With regard to whether Measure 3 was
adopted on the basis of this information, Panama itself indicates that this was not the case, by
asserting that it adopted the measure on the basis of two pieces of information concerning Costa
Rica's phytosanitary status in respect of the pest: (a) the presence of the pest in Costa Rica; and
(b) the absence of information on the phytosanitary status of pineapple-producing areas in Costa
Rica.2025 According to Panama, the fact that the pest was present in Costa Rica implied a "risk that
the pink mealybug will continue to spread to other areas of Costa Rica in other hosts, including
pineapple".2026 Therefore, and given the absence of "further technical information"2027 that,
according to Panama, would have enabled it to assess that risk, Panama decided to suspend imports
of fresh pineapple from Costa Rica.
7.976. The Panel notes that Panama decided to adopt Measure 3, which prohibits imports and is
considered under ISPM 11 to be "of last resort"2028, despite knowing that the pink mealybug is a
pest with limited distribution in Costa Rica, under official control, that has not been detected in
pineapple-producing areas of Costa Rica, and that has not been intercepted. Moreover, Panama itself
has confirmed that it knew the status of the pest in Costa Rica had not changed since it was notified
in 2014.2029
7.977. The Panel finds nothing in the record to suggest that the information on Costa Rica's
phytosanitary status in respect of the pest would justify the decision to inactivate the PIR for
pineapple from Costa Rica, thereby preventing the importation of this product into Panama.
7.978. With regard to the lack of further technical data on the phytosanitary status of
pineapple-producing areas in Costa Rica in reference to the pink mealybug, the Panel refers to the
conclusions in the previous section on the necessary information according to ISPM 11.2030 As
explained in the examination of the first requirement of Article 5.7, this ISPM does not support the
need to have such information in order to assess the risk in question and to adopt the measure
appropriate to the level of risk determined when the pest has not been found to be present in
pineapple-producing areas.
7.979. In the Panel's view, the body of information on Costa Rica's phytosanitary status in respect
of the pest available to Panama in January 2019 does not support the adoption of Measure 3.
Accordingly, the Panel concludes that Panama has failed to demonstrate that it adopted Measure 3

ISPM 2 and ISPM 20
7.980. The third category of information that Costa Rica considers pertinent consists of ISPM 2 and
ISPM 20. For Costa Rica, these standards are pertinent because "they refer to 'emergency' actions
– which may lead to the adoption of provisional measures pending technical justification – and
establish when such measures may be taken".2031 Panama disagrees with Costa Rica on the
pertinence of these two ISPM, since they do not address the phytosanitary risk in question and, in
its view, accepting their pertinence would mean imposing the particular ALOP reflected in these
standards on all WTO Members, contrary to Article 3.3 of the SPS Agreement.2032
7.981. With regard to Panama's argument that the ISPM are not pertinent because they do not
address the phytosanitary risk in question, the Panel recalls that, with respect to Measure 1, it has
concluded that pertinent information within the meaning of Article 5.7 does not refer exclusively to
information that addresses the particular risk in question.2033 As explained above2034, in the Panel's
view, Article 5.7 would not a priori exclude the pertinence of international standards of a general
nature that address the management of a particular situation (e.g. non-conformity), even if such
standards do not specifically refer to the product or risk in question.
7.982. Pursuant to Annex A(3) to the SPS Agreement, the IPPC Secretariat is a relevant
international organization in matters of plant health. In addition, the Panel notes that, unlike the
provisions of Annex A(3)(a) to the SPS Agreement on Codex standards, Annex A(3)(c) refers in
generic terms to "international standards, guidelines and recommendations developed under the
auspices of the Secretariat of the [IPPC]", without referring to any particular aspect of the field of
"plant health".2035 In the Panel's view, this language confirms that the pertinence of such standards
is not contingent on their addressing particular pests or products, as implied by Panama's argument.
Accordingly, the Panel considers that the ISPM, as standards developed under the auspices of the
IPPC Secretariat, constitute information "from" that organization that could be considered
"pertinent" for the purposes of Article 5.7.

reserves emergency measures for "new or unexpected phytosanitary situations", while ISPM 20

7.990. In the first scenario, which concerns "[p]ests not previously assessed", ISPM 20 states that,
"[a]t the time of interception, they may be categorized as regulated pests on a preliminary basis
because the NPPO has a cause to believe they pose a pest risk".2047 In the second scenario, which
deals with "[p]ests not regulated for a particular pathway", ISPM 20 refers implicitly to the
interception of the pest by stating that such pests "should be included on the appropriate list or
within other measure if it is determined that the occurrence of the pest in the same and similar
circumstances may be anticipated in the future".2048 In the Panel's view, this language indicates that
the emergency phytosanitary actions referred to in this scenario may be applied to non-regulated
pests in respect of particular pathways where it is determined that they are present in a shipment.
Lastly, the third scenario, which addresses the "[l]ack of adequate identification" of a pest, also
explicitly links emergency actions to pest detection by establishing how to proceed "[w]here pests
are routinely detected in a form that does not allow for adequate identification".2049
7.991. The context provided by other sections of ISPM 20, and by other ISPM and the IPPC, which
will be discussed below, appears to confirm this understanding that the concept of new, unforeseen
or unexpected situations is "commonly"2050 linked to the detection of pests in imported
consignments. Section 5.1.6.4 of ISPM 20 on "Withdrawal or modification of phytosanitary
regulation" provides that the NPPO of the importing contracting party may institute an emergency
or provisional measure in "the case of repeated non-compliance, or where a significant
non-compliance or interception warranting emergency action occurs".2051 In this regard, it should be
noted that the detection of regulated pests may be considered a significant instance of
non-compliance, as indicated in ISPM 13 on "Guidelines for the notification of non-compliance and
emergency action".2052
7.992. This same ISPM provides guidance for the notification of emergency measures related to the
failure of an imported consignment to comply with requirements or the detection of pests or
organisms therein. As indicated by Costa Rica2053, ISPM 13 establishes that emergency actions are
taken "on the detection in an imported consignment of … regulated pests" or "organisms posing a
potential phytosanitary threat".2054 The Panel also agrees with Costa Rica on the pertinence of
Article VII.6 of the IPPC2055, which confirms the above by establishing the right of any contracting
party to "tak[e] appropriate emergency action on the detection of a pest posing a potential threat
to its territories or the report of such a detection".2056
7.993. Having said this, the Panel agrees with Panama that the scenarios described in
section 5.1.6.2 of ISPM 20 do not constitute an exhaustive list of situations that may warrant the
adoption of an emergency action. This is evident from the use of expressions like "a new or
unexpected phytosanitary situation, such as"2057 and "[c]ommonly encountered situations requiring
emergency action include".2058 Therefore, the Panel does not rule out the possibility of scenarios not
explicitly envisaged in ISPM 20 that are not linked to the detection of a pest and that require the
adoption of emergency measures. Nevertheless, the scenarios discussed above, which are explicitly
identified in section 5.1.6.2 of ISPM 20, are linked to the detection of a pest. Since Panama asserts
that Measure 3 fits into one of these scenarios, namely that of "[p]ests not regulated for a particular
pathway", Measure 3 should result from the detection of the pest. However, the record contains no
evidence of the pest having been intercepted in shipments of Costa Rican pineapples.2059

7.997. The Panel recalls that Article 5.7 allows Members to adopt SPS measures provisionally "on
the basis of available pertinent information, including that from the relevant international
organizations as well as from sanitary or phytosanitary measures applied by other Members".2068
The Panel therefore considers that the measures adopted by other Members identified by Costa Rica
could be considered pertinent information for the purposes of the second requirement of Article 5.7
of the SPS Agreement. While Article 5.7 does not refer explicitly to measures of the Member adopting
the provisional measure, the measures adopted by Panama may also be pertinent to the risk in
question. The fact that the list of available pertinent information in Article 5.7 is not exhaustive, as
denoted by the use of the term "including", would permit the consideration of not only the categories
of information mentioned therein but also other information deemed pertinent to the risk in question
that is available to the Member adopting the provisional measure.
7.998. Costa Rica considers that these measures are pertinent, even if they relate to fruit other
than pineapples, because they concern risks arising from the pink mealybug pest.2069 For its part,
Panama does not consider them pertinent because, in its view, they are not related to the
phytosanitary risk in question or were adopted in circumstances different from those of the present
case.2070
7.999. With respect to Panama's argument that the measures of other Members applied to products
other than pineapple are not pertinent because they are not related to the phytosanitary risk in
question2071, the Panel agrees with Costa Rica that the measures concerning the importation of
avocados are pertinent, as both pineapple and avocado are considered to be hosts of the pest.2072
As a result, countries that import these products face the risk of transmission of the pest through
imports of those products. In addition, the Panel observes that the scientific literature on the pest
does not distinguish between hosts when addressing issues such as the detection and identification
of the pest, spread pathways, or control methods.2073
7.1000. The Panel also disagrees with Panama's position that some measures of other Members
and of Panama itself are not pertinent because they were adopted in circumstances different from
those of the present case with regard to the risk assessment in question. Panama refers specifically

language of the provision does not allow any measure applied by a Member to be excluded a priori.
In the Panel's view, the pertinence of the measure in question should be determined on a
case-by-case basis, and in the light of all relevant facts and circumstances.

7.1034. The Panel will now consider Costa Rica's claims under Articles 5.1, 5.2, 5.3, and 2.2 with

Whether Measure 3 is based on a risk assessment in accordance with Article 5.1 of the
SPS Agreement
7.1035. Panama has confirmed that Measure 3 is not based on a risk assessment, arguing that it is
a provisional measure that was adopted in a situation in which the body of available scientific
evidence did not allow an appropriate assessment of the risks to be performed, as required under
Article 5.1 and as defined in Annex A to the SPS Agreement.2139
7.1036. The Panel considers that, as claimed by Costa Rica, a measure cannot be based on a risk
assessment if no such assessment exists. Accordingly, the Panel finds that Measure 3 is inconsistent
with Article 5.1 of the SPS Agreement in that it is not based on an assessment, as appropriate to
the circumstances, of the risks to plant life or health, taking into account risk assessment techniques
developed by the relevant international organizations.
Whether Panama took into account the elements and factors listed in Articles 5.2 and 5.3
in the assessment of the risk
7.1037. As mentioned in paragraph 7.1032 above, Articles 5.2 and 5.3 are linked to Article 5.1, in
that they shed light on the elements and factors that are of relevance in the assessment of risks
foreseen in Article 5.1. Given that, in the case of Measure 3, Panama failed to conduct an assessment
of the risk, the Panel finds that Measure 3 is inconsistent with Articles 5.2 and 5.3 of the
SPS Agreement, as Panama did not take into account the elements and factors contained therein in
the assessment of the risks.
Whether Measure 3 is based on scientific principles and is not maintained without
sufficient scientific evidence in accordance with Article 2.2 of the SPS Agreement
7.1038. The Panel recalls that Article 5.1 constitutes a "specific application" of the basic obligations
under Article 2.2 of the SPS Agreement.2140 The Panel shares the view expressed in previous
disputes that where a measure is not based on a risk assessment pursuant to Article 5.1 of the
SPS Agreement, it can be presumed not to be based on scientific principles or to be maintained
without sufficient scientific evidence within the meaning of Article 2.2.2141 The Panel considers that
this presumption can be made in the present case because of its finding that, in the absence of a
risk assessment, Measure 3 is inconsistent with Articles 5.1, 5.2, and 5.3.2142 The Panel further notes
that Panama has failed to submit arguments to rebut this presumption.
7.1039. Accordingly, in the light of its finding that Measure 3 is not based on an assessment of the
risk, in breach of Articles 5.1, 5.2, and 5.3 of the SPS Agreement, and in the absence of a rebuttal
by Panama concerning the presumption of inconsistency with Article 2.2 of the Agreement, the Panel
finds that Measure 3 is inconsistent with Article 2.2 because it is not based on scientific principles
and is maintained without sufficient scientific evidence.

7.5.1.3.2.1 Relevant legal standard
7.1048. As explained in the context of Measure 2, Article 2.3 of the SPS Agreement contains two
different obligations. The first sentence of Article 2.3 requires that SPS measures do not arbitrarily
or unjustifiably discriminate between Members where identical or similar conditions prevail, including
between their own territory and that of other Members. The second sentence of Article 2.3 requires
that SPS measures shall not be applied in a manner which would constitute a disguised restriction
on international trade.2161
7.1049. The Panel recalls that, to establish a violation of the first sentence of Article 2.3, Costa Rica
must demonstrate three cumulative elements:
a. the measure discriminates between the territories of Members other than Panama, or
between Panama's territory and that of another Member;
b. the discrimination is arbitrary or unjustifiable; and
c. identical or similar conditions prevail in the territory of the Members compared.2162
7.1050. With respect to the second sentence of Article 2.3, the Panel recalls that a disguised
restriction on international trade has been considered to encompass measures that constitute
arbitrary or unjustifiable discrimination.2163

provision.2164

7.1066. The Panel identifies three main issues in the arguments of the parties, which it will now
address. These issues concern: (a) the differences in the PIR for avocado from Colombia and for
pineapple from Costa Rica in relation to the mitigation measures for the pink mealybug; (b) the

not with Panama's ALOP with respect to imports of these two products.
7.1067. With respect to the first issue, relating to the mitigation measures for the pink mealybug
set out in the relevant PIR, the Panel observes that Panama focuses on the fact that, unlike the PIR
for pineapple from Costa Rica, the PIR for avocado from Colombia provide for a mitigation measure
for the pink mealybug. This measure requires that the shipment has a phytosanitary certificate
issued by the Colombian Agricultural Institute (ICA) containing an additional declaration certifying
that the shipment is free from pink mealybug.2184
7.1068. Panama justifies this difference in the PIR for avocado and the PIR for pineapple on the
grounds that, when it adopted the PIR for avocado in 2007, it was aware of the presence of the pest
in Colombia since 2003, and considered that the risk of pest transmission was greater in avocado
imports from Colombia compared to pineapple imports from Costa Rica. Conversely, Panama notes
that, when it adopted the PIR for pineapple from Costa Rica in 2008, it was not aware of the presence
of the pest in Costa Rica given that it was notified for the first time several years later, in 2014.2185
7.1069. The Panel notes that the reason given by Panama for having included a mitigation measure
for the pink mealybug in the PIR for avocado is linked solely to its knowledge of Colombia's
phytosanitary status with respect to the pest, and not to other aspects such as detections of the
pest in shipments of avocados from Colombia2186 or the potential higher risk posed by avocado as a
main host of the pest.2187 This fits with Panama's explanation of how it drafts its PIR for foods of
plant origin intended for consumption. The Panel recalls that Panama has indicated that, in order to
draft these PIR, AUPSA "verified the pests of quarantine concern reported officially by the [NPPOs]
of each country of origin and compared them with the list of pests of Panama's NPPO, as well as its
ability to follow the pathway"2188, and that "[t]his verification was Panama's risk analysis, but it was
not documented as such."2189

include a mitigation measure for this pest in its PIR for avocado. However, when Panama was notified
about the presence of the pest in Costa Rica in May 2014, it did not modify the PIR for pineapple
from Costa Rica to include a mitigation measure, as it had done for avocados from Colombia. Panama
